## The question comes before the method

Together, the three papers make a case for treating causal inference first as a
discipline of question-setting. A causal question must say what intervention is
being compared with what alternative, for whom, over what period, and against
which outcome. Choosing a model before settling those points does not merely
leave details unspecified; it can change the question being answered.

Dickerman and colleagues provide the sharpest demonstration. Using electronic
health records from 733,804 UK adults, they compared statin initiation with no
initiation. An analysis that classified people by whether they accumulated more
than four years of statin use produced a hazard ratio of 0.22 for total cancer,
suggesting a very large protective association. The classification used future
information: to enter the long-term-user group, a person had to remain alive,
cancer-free and under follow-up long enough to accumulate that exposure. This
created immortal time bias.

When eligibility, treatment assignment and the start of follow-up were aligned
at time zero to emulate a target trial, the corresponding intention-to-treat
hazard ratio was 1.02. The same flaw reversed the apparent direction of the
association with type 2 diabetes: defining exposure by observed duration gave a
hazard ratio of 0.20, whereas the target-trial estimate was 1.11. The lesson is
not that observational data cannot support causal inference. It is that a large
dataset and a sophisticated analysis cannot repair a comparison defined using
information that would have been unavailable when treatment was assigned.

## Four targets expose what the estimate means

Lu and colleagues proposed four targets for causal inference on observation data. The **target
estimand** states the treatment effect of interest, including the intervention,
comparator, outcome and follow-up. The **target population** states to whom the
answer is intended to apply. The **target trial** is the hypothetical pragmatic
randomised trial the observational analysis seeks to emulate. **Target validity**
then asks whether the estimate is valid for that estimand and population,
combining the usual concerns about internal and external validity.

This framework shifts difficult conversations to the beginning of a study. “Do
statins prevent cancer?” is not yet a complete causal question: initiation and
sustained treatment are different interventions, dose and adherence require
definitions, and the relevant population and follow-up period must be fixed.
Changing these choices after seeing the result changes the estimand and invites
cherry-picking.

The discussion connected these targets to three identification assumptions.
**Consistency** requires the intervention and outcome to be defined well enough
that an observed treatment corresponds to the treatment being analysed.
**Positivity** requires both treatment strategies to be possible for every
relevant kind of participant. **Exchangeability** requires the comparison groups
not to differ, after conditioning on measured information, in other causes of
the outcome. Health-seeking behaviour illustrates the last problem: people who
take preventive medication may also seek care, undergo screening or change
behaviour in ways that affect their cancer risk.

Making assumptions explicit is useful, but does not make them true. An analysis
can therefore supply a causal answer only conditional on assumptions that data
alone may not verify. Disagreement about a causal conclusion may persist because
attendees accept different assumptions, rather than because one side has chosen
the wrong estimator.

## Cell experiments intervene, but design still sets the claim

The same reasoning applies to single-cell experiments without requiring every
study to adopt the machinery of observational epidemiology. A pathway-inhibition
experiment can specify an intervention, a matched control, an outcome at a fixed
time and a target population of donors. In that sense, experimental biologists
already reason causally whenever they perturb a system and compare outcomes.

The causal framing nevertheless reveals familiar failure modes. Cells are not
independent biological replicates when treatment is assigned at the donor or
culture level. Quality-control filtering can also become post-treatment
selection: if an intervention changes RNA abundance or cell viability, applying
the same threshold may selectively remove the cells most affected by treatment.
Finally, a result across a small set of donors does not automatically transport
to the population the biological claim names.

One unresolved point was whether formal causal inference is necessary for useful
biological or clinical work. Yeganeh Khazaei argued that action can be justified
by a sufficiently strong body of evidence without every study establishing a
causal effect in isolation. Others stressed that discovery experiments often
leave the question flexible and use a later perturbation as validation, which
does not necessarily reproduce a pre-specified target trial. Jiadong's proposed
middle ground was causal inference as an attitude to design: ask what would have
to be compared, make the assumptions visible, and state how far the resulting
claim can travel.

## Evidence does not come from one culture

Swales' three “cultures” supplied a broader account of evidence: mechanistic
biomedicine asks whether an intervention could work, clinical experience asks
how it behaves in whole patients, and numerical evidence estimates whether it
does work across groups. Each can correct the others. Homeopathy has had
apparently favourable numerical results without a credible mechanism or clinical
acceptance. Conversely, suppressing ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial
infarction had mechanistic and clinical plausibility, yet randomised evidence
showed that particular antiarrhythmic drugs increased mortality.

The biological analogue of clinical evidence remained unsettled. For cell and
animal studies it might include accumulated domain knowledge about the model,
the experimental design and the conditions under which results have previously
translated. It would not replace direct evidence in patients, but it still
constrains which causal accounts are plausible. No resolution was reached on how
the three cultures should be weighted, or on what their precise analogues are
outside clinical medicine.

Meta-analysis does not remove this design problem. Pooling studies that define
exposure, time zero or eligible populations incompatibly can make a biased answer
more precise. Yeganeh noted that when clinical studies are highly heterogeneous,
a systematic or scoping review may be more defensible than forcing a pooled
estimate. Inclusion criteria and the target question must therefore be settled
before synthesis, just as they must be settled before modelling a single cohort.

## Follow-up reading

Yeganeh proposed adaptive platform trials as a practical extension to the
discussion. These trials use a master protocol to evaluate several interventions
and can add or drop arms under pre-specified decision rules. A general entry point
is Angus DC, Alexander BM, Berry S, *et al.* *Adaptive platform trials:
definition, design, conduct and reporting considerations.* Nature Reviews Drug
Discovery 18:797–807 (2019).
[doi:10.1038/s41573-019-0034-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41573-019-0034-3)
